evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire chartbook is built around MyLymeData, a patient-driven registry of individuals clinically diagnosed with Lyme disease, and its content (symptoms, diagnosis, co-infections, treatment, access barriers, quality of life, healthcare utilization, gender differences) is entirely about Lyme disease and persistent Lyme disease (PLD). Long COVID is mentioned only once, in passing, as an example of another condition under the 'Lyme IACI' umbrella term, with no Long COVID data, population, or figures analyzed.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a 10-year anniversary research chartbook from LymeDisease.org's MyLymeData patient registry (19,000+ self-enrolled, clinically diagnosed Lyme disease patients). It reports patient-reported rates of diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis, co-infections, treatment approaches, insurance and access barriers, clinician-reported practice burdens, quality-of-life decline, and healthcare utilization, focused mainly on 'persistent Lyme disease' (PLD) patients who remain ill 6+ months after treatment. It presents these largely as percentages from registry surveys rather than as dollar-denominated cost estimates, with one externally cited claims-based study estimating roughly $1 billion/year in U.S. healthcare costs tied to retreatment of diagnosed Lyme patients. The chartbook explicitly frames itself as advocacy/research-prioritization material produced by a patient organization, not an independent economic burden-of-illness study.

contextual_issues: Patient quotes describe severe uncompensated personal financial losses (lost job, retirement savings, social life) but these are individual anecdotes, not aggregated or quantified across the registry.
A higher risk of suicide associated with Lyme borreliosis is mentioned (citing Fallon et al. 2021) without a document-specific rate or population figure.

The document cites the general claim that '80% of the cost of chronic illness is productivity losses,' a generic chronic-illness statistic not specific to Lyme disease and not applied to compute a Lyme-specific dollar figure.
The generic claim that 'chronic illnesses account for 84% of healthcare costs' is cited as general background, not a Lyme- or PLD-specific cost estimate.

Caregiver time, travel costs, and non-medical out-of-pocket costs (lodging, lost wages from travel) are implied by the 32%-travel-100+-miles finding but not separately quantified in dollar or time terms.
Co-infection-specific treatment costs are discussed qualitatively (co-infections 'must be treated individually') without a cost figure.

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine is quoted stating that patient registries and biobanks are 'underused' in Lyme infection-associated chronic illness (IACI) research, a systemic/qualitative observation not quantified.

Historic randomized controlled trials for persistent Lyme disease are described as including 'only 37 to 129 patients,' illustrating a small-sample limitation without a single quantifiable burden figure.
evidence_gaps: No direct patient out-of-pocket spending or total dollar cost figures from the MyLymeData registry itself; healthcare utilization is reported as visit counts (e.g., 19.4 annual doctor visits) without attached unit costs.
No lifetime or multi-year cost projection is provided or attempted; all figures are either single time-point percentages or the single Adrion et al. 2015 claims-based annual aggregate figure.

No breakdown of healthcare utilization, cost, or access-barrier findings by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status; only sex/gender and disease-stage (ALD/PLD) and treatment-responder subgroups are reported.

The Adrion et al. 2015 $1 billion/year estimate is drawn from insurance claims of diagnosed Lyme patients, which by the document's own account (50% of PLD patients' physicians do not accept insurance) likely excludes an unknown share of PLD patients who pay out of pocket or see non-billing clinicians.

No formal comparison or reconciliation is offered between the CDC's ~500,000 cases/year estimate, the DeLong 2019 cumulative 2 million PLD estimate, and MyLymeData's own registry-based percentages, despite all three bearing on the same underlying disease burden.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the CDC's cited estimate of ~500,000 annual Lyme disease cases (no stated year, national, all Lyme disease) with DeLong et al. 2019's cumulative estimate of 2 million Americans with post-treatment/persistent Lyme disease (PLD specifically, cumulative not annual) - these differ in case definition, population, and time horizon.

Do not pool the 72% PLD fair/poor-health figure attributed to DeLong 2019 (compared against a 13% general-population baseline) with the separately reported 72% PLD fair/poor-health figure from Johnson et al. 2014 (compared against a 16% general-population baseline) - these are two different studies/surveys with different general-population comparators, even though the PLD-side number happens to match.

Do not pool MyLymeData's self-reported healthcare utilization counts (e.g., 19.4 annual doctor visits, patient self-report via MEPS-style survey items) with the Adrion et al. 2015 insurance-claims-based $1 billion/year cost estimate - these use different data sources (patient self-report registry vs. insured-claims database), different populations (all registry PLD patients, including the ~50% whose providers do not accept insurance, vs. only insurance-claims-captured patients), and different units (utilization counts vs. aggregate dollars).

Do not conflate 'persistent Lyme disease' (PLD) as defined by MyLymeData (clinical diagnosis plus ongoing symptoms ≥6 months post-treatment) with the academic research term 'Post-Treatment Lyme Disease' (PTLD), which the document states excludes about 90% of patients who would otherwise meet the PLD definition - these are structurally different, non-interchangeable populations.

Do not treat acute Lyme disease (ALD) and persistent Lyme disease (PLD) statistics (e.g., misdiagnosis rate, disability rate, co-infection rate) as a single pooled Lyme disease figure - the document consistently reports them as distinct disease-stage subgroups with large differences.

The quality-of-life comparison across diseases (PLD, multiple sclerosis, diabetes, fibromyalgia, congestive heart failure, depression, general population) on page 21 is a self-rated-health-status comparison only (Johnson et al. 2014); it is not a cost comparison and should not be treated as evidence of comparative economic burden across those conditions.

sex_gender_findings.finding: A MyLymeData-partnered study of over 2,000 PLD patients (Johnson et al. 2023) found that women reported more tick-borne co-infections, longer diagnostic delays, greater symptom severity, and worse functional impairment than men, and were more likely to be misdiagnosed (particularly with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric disorders) than men. The document states no differences were reported between sexes in antibiotic treatment response or side effects. Separately, 85% of MyLymeData registry participants are women.
sex_gender_findings.source_locator: page 28-29 (Gender Differences section; Johnson et al. 2023)

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The $1 billion/year U.S. healthcare cost figure attributed to Dr. Emily Adrion's study is explicitly described in the document as derived from 'insurance claims records of over 50,000 Lyme patients' (Adrion et al. 2015) - an insurance-claims-based data source, which the document itself notes elsewhere only captures insured services and would miss the roughly 50% of PLD patients whose providers do not accept insurance.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The ~$1 billion/year Adrion et al. 2015 healthcare cost estimate for Lyme disease patients, and the DeLong et al. 2019 cumulative estimate of 2 million Americans with persistent Lyme disease, are both presented as single national pooled figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a gap between a large, growing population of persistent Lyme disease patients and the research/clinical infrastructure available to treat them: it states 'despite the growing number of these cases, very little research has been conducted on how best to treat them,' identifies inadequate physician education about tick-borne disease as the leading cited cause (86%) of diagnostic delay, notes only 4% of PLD patients are seen by infectious disease specialists, and quotes the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine stating that patient registries and biobanks are 'underused' in Lyme infection-associated chronic illness research.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Overview section (page 7, 'very little research has been conducted'); reasons for delayed diagnosis table (page 17, 86% inadequate physician education); patient barriers to care section (page 19, only 4% seen by infectious disease specialists); National Academies quote on page 25.

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would let patients/advocates, care delivery teams, and payers/policy audiences explore how diagnostic timing, misdiagnosis, co-infection status, and insurance-network barriers relate to self-reported quality of life, disability, and healthcare utilization among persistent Lyme disease (PLD) patients. Because the document's own figures are overwhelmingly percentages from a self-selected patient registry rather than linked dollar costs, the simulator's main value is illustrating burden patterns (delay-to-PLD-risk, access barriers, utilization intensity) rather than producing validated total-cost estimates. Payers/policy users could use the access-barrier and insurance-non-acceptance findings to examine network-adequacy questions; care teams could use the co-infection and symptom-severity findings to inform diagnostic workup prioritization; patients/advocates could see how registry-reported experiences compare to general-population and other chronic-disease benchmarks.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could use the registry's early-vs-late diagnosis PLD-progression rates (20% of early-diagnosed vs 77% of late-diagnosed patients developing PLD) to illustrate, qualitatively, why earlier diagnosis is emphasized by the patient community - without implying a validated causal estimate.

Payers/policy analysts could examine the gap between PLD patients' reported care intensity (19.4 annual doctor visits, 3.7 annual ER visits) and the clinician-reported insurance-access barriers (50% of patients' physicians do not accept insurance; ~75% of surveyed Lyme-treating clinicians do not participate in insurance networks) to inform network-adequacy or reimbursement policy discussions.

Care delivery teams could use the co-infection prevalence difference (33% in acute patients vs 75% in PLD patients) to evaluate whether earlier co-infection testing protocols might be warranted, consistent with the document's own hedged framing ('may be a primary driver').

package.documentation:
## Source
This simulator is built from LymeDisease.org's MyLymeData 10-year anniversary chartbook, based on a self-enrolled, clinically diagnosed patient registry (19,000+ participants). It is an advocacy and research-prioritization publication, not an independent economic burden-of-illness study. Most figures are patient- or clinician-reported percentages; only one dollar figure (an externally cited claims-based study) is included.

## Inputs and sources
- Early- vs. late-diagnosis persistent-disease rates and persistent- vs. acute-disease misdiagnosis rates come from page 17 and page 7 of the chartbook, self-reported by registry participants.
- Annual doctor-visit figures (page 23) are self-reported by registry participants using MEPS-style survey items; MEPS itself does not support Lyme-specific cost analysis and is not used here as a cost source.
- The insurance non-acceptance rate (page 15) and the Adrion et al. 2015 cost estimate (page 23) are reported directly in the chartbook.

## Limitations
**Claims undercounting**: the roughly $1 billion/year healthcare cost figure is drawn from insurance claims records of diagnosed Lyme patients (Adrion et al. 2015). Because the chartbook itself reports that about half of persistent Lyme disease patients' physicians do not accept insurance, this claims-based figure likely undercounts true healthcare costs for this population.

**Subgroup disaggregation**: the $1 billion/year cost estimate, and separately a cited cumulative estimate of 2 million Americans with persistent Lyme disease, are both pooled national figures not broken down by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroups in this document. Federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it. The chartbook does separately report that women in a partnered study (Johnson et al. 2023) reported more co-infections, longer diagnostic delays, greater symptom severity, and more frequent misdiagnosis (particularly with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric conditions) than men, with no reported sex difference in antibiotic treatment response or side effects; 85% of registry participants are women.

**Systemic gap**: the chartbook describes a gap between the growing persistent Lyme disease population and available clinical/research infrastructure - 86% of surveyed Lyme-treating clinicians cited inadequate physician education about tick-borne disease as a cause of diagnostic delay, only 4% of persistent-disease patients are seen by infectious disease specialists, and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine is quoted describing patient registries and biobanks as 'underused' in this research area.

## Boundary
All diagnosis-timing, misdiagnosis, and utilization comparisons are associations reported within a self-selected registry; the document does not establish that earlier diagnosis causes lower persistent-disease risk or that misdiagnosis causes worse outcomes.

inputs.source: MyLymeData chartbook page 23, citing Adrion et al. 2015 (external claims-based study, not MyLymeData's own estimate); 500,000,000-1,500,000,000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the externally cited claims-based estimate of annual U.S. healthcare cost from retreatment of diagnosed Lyme patients. Moving it explores sensitivity of the headline cost output; it does not change the registry's own percentage-based findings.

outputs.label: Persistent-disease rate gap: late-diagnosed minus early-diagnosed patients (positive = later diagnosis associated with higher reported persistent-disease rate)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the share of late-diagnosed and early-diagnosed MyLymeData patients who reported developing persistent Lyme disease. A larger positive value reflects a bigger reported difference between these two groups; the document reports this as an association observed within the registry, not a controlled test of whether earlier diagnosis prevents persistent disease.

outputs.label: Misdiagnosis-rate gap: persistent Lyme disease minus acute Lyme disease patients (positive = persistent-disease group reports more pre-Lyme misdiagnosis)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the share of persistent-disease and acute-disease registry patients who reported being misdiagnosed before their Lyme diagnosis. A larger positive value means persistent-disease patients in this registry reported substantially more pre-diagnosis misdiagnosis than acute-disease patients; the document presents this as a registry-reported pattern, not a causal estimate of how misdiagnosis produces persistent illness.

outputs.label: Ratio of persistent Lyme disease patients' annual doctor visits to the general-population comparator
outputs.interpretation: This is how many times more annual doctor visits persistent-disease registry patients self-reported compared to the cited general-population figure. A higher ratio means greater self-reported care-seeking intensity among persistent-disease patients relative to the general population in this comparison; it does not by itself indicate cost, since visit counts and dollar costs are not linked in this source.

outputs.label: Persistent Lyme disease patients reporting their physician does not accept insurance
outputs.interpretation: This restates the registry's reported share of persistent-disease patients whose physician does not accept insurance. A higher value means more registry patients faced this specific access barrier when seeking treating clinicians, per the document's own account.

outputs.label: Estimated annual U.S. healthcare cost tied to Lyme disease retreatment (claims-based, cited)
outputs.interpretation: This is the externally cited Adrion et al. 2015 claims-based estimate of annual U.S. healthcare cost from Lyme disease retreatment, carried through unchanged from the source. Because it is based on insurance claims, it likely undercounts true healthcare costs for Lyme and persistent Lyme disease patients, given the registry's own finding that about half of persistent-disease patients' physicians do not accept insurance.
